text: You get the root of a binary tree. Return true if it's a valid binary search tree.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — valid means every node in the whole left subtree is strictly smaller than the node, and every node in the whole right subtree is strictly bigger. Not just the direct children. And both subtrees must be search trees too, so duplicates are not allowed anywhere. Is that right?
Yes. Strictly less on the left, strictly greater on the right.
Got it. Are there any constraints on the input size?
There are one to ten to the fourth nodes, and a node value can be anything from negative two to the thirty-first, up to two to the thirty-first minus one.

Okay, two things jump out. The tree isn't promised to be balanced, so it could be a chain ten thousand deep. And the values use the entire int range, including int min and int max — that will matter when I pick no-limit values. The key fact: every node lives inside an open range, L to R, that comes from all of its ancestors, not just its parent. Going left, the parent's value becomes the new upper bound; going right, it becomes the new lower bound. Quick check on example two: five, one, four, null, null, three, six. Four is the right child of five, so it must be bigger than five. It isn't, so the answer is false. That matches.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would be to check each node only against its two children. It's tempting, but it's wrong. The smallest breaking input has three nodes: two, null, three, one. One is the left child of three, so it looks fine locally. But one sits in two's right subtree, so it must be bigger than two, and it isn't. This problem reminds me of passing constraints down a recursion: each call gets the range its node must fit in. The other classic idea is that an inorder walk of a search tree is strictly increasing. Both are linear time. I'll go with the bounds version, because it states the rule directly and it can stop at the first bad node.

Here's the plan. One: a helper takes a node and an open range, L to R, and a null node is valid. Two: fail if the node's value is not strictly inside the range. Three: recurse left with the node's value as the new upper bound, and right with it as the new lower bound. The other side carries through unchanged — that's how a limit from high up reaches deep nodes. One thing worth flagging — the infinity values. Node values fill the whole int range, so any int sentinel is also a real value. With int min and a strict check, a single node holding int min returns false. Switch to less-or-equal, and duplicates like one, null, one slip through. So the sentinel must live outside int: I'll use sixty-four-bit bounds. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. The public function just starts the helper with the widest bounds. The helper does the range check, then recurses left with the node's value as the new top, and right with it as the new floor. The and-chain short-circuits: once a check fails, nothing after it runs. One thing worth flagging — I wrote long min and long max. On sixty-four-bit Linux, long is eight bytes, so that's fine. But on Windows with MSVC, long is only thirty-two bits, so long min equals int min, and we're back to the int bug. The portable fix is long long min and long long max. Another option is node-pointer bounds, with null meaning no limit — no sentinel at all.

Let's dry-run the code on a case where the limit comes from a grandparent: five, four, six, null, null, three, seven. I expect false. The row that matters is node three. It's the left child of six, and three is less than six, so locally it looks fine. But the lower bound five was set by the root and carried down through six unchanged. Five less than three fails, so the answer is false, and seven is never visited. That's exactly what the children-only check misses. Corner cases: a single node holding int min or int max returns true, because the bounds are sixty-four-bit. One, null, one returns false, since a duplicate isn't strictly greater. And two, null, three, one returns false — the three-node trap.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is linear: each node gets one call doing constant work. On a valid tree that's exactly two n plus one calls, counting null children. On an invalid tree the short-circuit can stop very early — if the root's left child is broken, it's just two calls, no matter the size. Space is O of h for the recursion stack. Worst case is a chain, ten thousand and one frames deep. On an eight megabyte stack, the crash only comes at about a hundred seventy-four thousand frames, a seventeen-times margin, so recursion is fine here. Oh, one more thing — why a separate helper instead of default arguments? With defaults, a caller could pass zero and ten by mistake, and the valid tree twenty, ten, thirty would return false. A helper means the public function can only be called the right way.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You showed early that each node needs a range from all its ancestors, and broke the children-only check with two, null, three, one. You explained why the bounds must be sixty-four-bit, with a lone int min node and one, null, one as the two ways an int sentinel fails. And you caught that long min is only safe where long is sixty-four-bit, and gave long long min or null-pointer bounds as the fix. Good work.
